newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Three U.S. scientists win 1996 Nobel Physics Prize.
newsitem.headline: Three U.S. scientists win 1996 Nobel Physics Prize.

text.p: Three U.S. scientists whose work inspired colleagues trying to unlock the mysteries of the universe were awarded the 1996 Nobel Physics Prize, the Royal Swedish Acadaemy of Sciences said on Wednesday.
David Lee, Douglas Osheroff and Robert Richardson shared the the prize, worth $1.12 million, for their quantum physics discovery about the superfluidity of the helium-3 isotope.
They made their breakthrough in low-temperature physics in the early 1970s at Cornell University in the state of New York.
"I am overwhelmed and very, very happy." Lee told Swedish national news agency TT by telephone from Cornell University.
"We knew we had made a very important discovery, but none of us had expected this, at least not this year," he added.

Lee, born in 1931 in Rye, New York, and Richardson, born in 1937 in Washington D.C., both work in Cornell's Department of Physics. Osheroff, born in Aberdeen, Washington, in 1945, works at the Department of Physics at California's Stanford University.
Nobel committee member Mats Jonson told Reuters there were similarities between the helium-3 superfluid and theories about early stages of the universe and how galaxies formed.
Jonson said later experiments on helium-3 systems had shed light on the evolution of the universe immediately after the so-called "Big Bang".
"This work has given us a better toolbox for understanding other phenomena such as high-temperature superconductivity, such as cosmic strings and early development of the universe," he said.
The academy said the three men discovered that the helium isotope helium-3 can be made superfluid at a temperature only about two thousandths of a degree above absolute zero.

Superfluidity is a scientific term for when a liquid is made so cold it loses all its usual molecular patterns shortly before it reaches the stage of absolute zero at minus 273.15 degrees centigrade (-459.67F -- Absolute zero -459.68F).
When a liquid becomes superfluid its atoms lose all their randomness; the liquid can overflow a cup or flow out through a very small hole and exhibit a range of bizarre characteristics.
At such low temperatures the atoms of the helium-3 isotope no longer behave independently, Jonson said.
"All the motion of the helium-3 atom gets coordinated so they move together in a way and the system become superfluid -- it flows very easily, without any resistance, without any viscosity."

An inexperienced graduate student at the time, Osheroff first noticed a tiny blip in a chart from an impromptu experiment, but had to convince his collaborators, who were senior researchers, of the discovery's significance.
"Osheroff...must have been 25 or 26 years old and he was sitting around and he thought he'd do something to get to know the apparatus," Jonson told Reuters.

"He noticed some glitches in the measurement curve, which could be due to a lot of things -- like something wrong with the apparatus or he was coughing of something...That actually turned out to be the real result."
The three scientists' discoveries was a major advance on helium-4, which becomes superfluid at temperatures around one thousand times higher than helium-3.
"The discovery heralded the start of intensive research on the new quantum liquid," the academy said.
